draft.title: Science communication
card: Science communication is how science is shared with the public, in news stories, ads and social media posts.
What people read can shape what they believe and what they do, such as whether they choose a product or follow health advice.
It can also shape the rules governments make, because leaders and voters often rely on how science is reported.
Good science communication is clear and based on evidence. A claim with no source, or one that leaves out how it was tested, is harder to trust.
draft.remember: How science is reported can shape beliefs and rules, so it should be clear and based on evidence.

a.q: Why should science be reported clearly and with evidence?
opts: Reports shape what people believe and what rules are made
Reports decide which experiments scientists carry out next
Reports make sure that every claim in them is true
Reports are only read by scientists and government leaders
a.why: Many people use reports to decide what to believe and do, and governments may use them when making rules. Clear, evidence-based reports help those choices. Reports do not make a claim true: the evidence has to be sound.
a.clue: Think about who reads reports and what they do next.

b.q: An ad for a drink says in large letters, "Scientists say it boosts your brain!" It names no study and gives no details. What is the best response?
opts: Ask what evidence supports the claim before believing it
Believe it, because the ad mentions scientists
Ignore it, because ads can never use real science
Believe it, because the words are in large letters
b.why: The ad gives no source or detail, so the claim cannot be checked. The best step is to ask for the evidence. Saying that ads can never use real science is also wrong: some ads do, so each claim should be judged on its evidence.
b.clue: Can you check a claim that names no study?

a.best: Reports shape what people believe and what rules are made

b.best: Ask what evidence supports the claim before believing it
